VIDEO.title: You're Asking God the Wrong Question About Suffering
VIDEO.series: The Book of Hebrews, Every Word (playlist in progress)

kicker: Study aid · Hebrews 2:9-18 · Episode 3 (#3 of 4 so far in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher opens with a question: what if you've misunderstood what God is doing when He doesn't take your suffering away? Most of us pray for it to stop, and that's not wrong, but Hebrews 2 says something about Christ's suffering that many overlook, and he has wrestled with it for 17 years. He reads Hebrews 2:9-18: we see Jesus, made for a little while lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death; God perfects the author of salvation through sufferings; He is not ashamed to call us brothers; He shared flesh and blood to render the devil powerless and free those enslaved by fear of death; He was made like His brothers to be a merciful and faithful high priest.

Observations: 'But we do see Him' answers 2:8. We don't yet see humanity ruling as Psalm 8 describes, but we see Jesus, the true, representative human who fulfills mankind's destiny. His suffering and death were 'by the grace of God', the sovereign, gracious plan of God, not an accident. In verse 10 the subject is God the Father: 'it was fitting' points back to 'by the grace of God'. Yet Hebrews 1 ties creation to the Son, so the author assumes both distinction and unity in God without stopping to explain; the teacher points to the 'two powers in heaven' discussion (Alan Segal; popularized by Michael Heiser).

'Perfect' doesn't mean Christ was flawed, but that He completed something: bringing many sons to glory through suffering. The Son is not ashamed to call weak, tempted people brothers. Verse 14 describes the incarnation, and verse 15's slavery, death and deliverance has a new-Exodus flavor, preparing for Moses in chapter 3: Jesus is the greater deliverer. Verse 17's priestly language presents Him as the merciful and faithful high priest who makes propitiation.

Old Testament background: Psalm 8 is still the backdrop for verse 9, and the logic tracks with Romans 5:17, Adam's trespass and the reign of the One, Jesus Christ. Psalm 22, which Jesus quoted on the cross, moves from suffering to vindication and praise among the brothers (2:12). Isaiah and his children were signs in Israel during fear and political crisis, when people were tempted to fear earthly powers rather than trust Yahweh (2:13). Israel's priesthood, sacrifice and atonement stand behind 2:17. In one word, the passage is about solidarity.

The lesson: 'Suffering is not a detour from human glory. In union with the Son who suffered with us and for us, suffering becomes part of the path by which God brings many sons to glory.' For pressured, weary believers, suffering did not mean God had abandoned them or that Jesus had failed.
QUOTES: Suffering is not a detour from human glory. In union with the Son who suffered with us and for us, suffering becomes part of the path by which God brings many sons to glory.
Jesus is the representative human being. He entered into our lowly condition.
If I had to summarize this movement in the text in one word, I would say it's solidarity.
Lord, meet me here. Form Christ in me right here. And if you do not remove this suffering today, don't let it be wasted.

method.p: In Hebrews 2:9-11 mark every 'He', 'Him' and 'His' and decide who each refers to: the Father, the Son, or the brothers. Then do the same in 1:1-3 and see how the author speaks of the Father and the Son together.

PRIEST.title: A merciful and faithful high priest

left.text: “Then he shall slaughter the goat of the sin offering which is for the people and bring its blood inside the veil and do with its blood as he did with the blood of the bull. And he shall sprinkle it on the mercy seat and in front of the mercy seat.

right.text: Therefore, He had to be made like His brothers in all things, so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.

lines.text: The language recalls Aaron's priesthood, sacrifice, mediation and atonement: the high priest represented the people before God. Later the author will say Jesus is greater, because He does not offer a sacrifice outside Himself; He gives Himself. Because He suffered when tempted, 'He is able to come to help those who are tempted' (Hebrews 2:18).

TERMS.def: To complete or bring to the goal, not to fix a flaw (2:10).
The Son taking on flesh and blood (2:14).
The sacrifice that turns away God's wrath and deals with sin (2:17).
God's greater deliverance, patterned on the rescue from Egypt.
Ancient Jewish discussion of a second divine figure alongside Yahweh; studied by Alan Segal.
The teacher's one-word summary: Jesus fully shares our condition.

BACKGROUND.p: Israel's high priest represented the people before God and, on the Day of Atonement, brought sacrificial blood into the most holy place (Leviticus 16). Hebrews introduces Jesus as high priest here and develops it from chapter 4 on.

BACKGROUND.h: Fear of death in the ancient world
BACKGROUND.p: Death was feared across the ancient world, and philosophers wrote to help people face it. Hebrews names fear of death as a slavery that Jesus breaks by entering death Himself.

Alan Segal's study traced rabbinic objections to teachers who spoke of a second divine power in heaven. Michael Heiser argued the idea has roots in the Old Testament itself, where Yahweh can be distinguished from Yahweh.

DEBATES.p: Hilaskomai can mean turning away God's wrath (propitiation, as in the LSB) or wiping away sin (expiation). C. H. Dodd argued for expiation; many since have argued that both ideas are present.

Interpreters agree it isn't moral improvement. Some stress vocational completion (qualified as Savior and priest through suffering); others stress His human obedience reaching its goal in death and exaltation.

Chrysostom read 'taste death for everyone' as the whole world. Others read it within the letter's focus on the 'many sons' and 'brothers'. The verse figures in wider debates about the scope of the atonement.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small points worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says both quotations in 2:13 come from Isaiah 8:17. The second, 'Behold, I and the children', is Isaiah 8:18. The first follows the Greek of 8:17; the LSB, translating the Hebrew, reads 'I will hope for Him'.
The video reads Psalm 8:5 as 'a little lower than the heavenly beings'; the LSB, like Hebrews 2:9, has 'angels'. The Hebrew word ('elohim) allows both.

QUESTIONS: What do you usually pray first when you or someone you love is suffering?
How does 'we do see Him' (2:9) answer 'we do not yet see' (2:8)?
What does it mean that Jesus was 'perfected' without ever being flawed?
Where do you need to hear that the Son is not ashamed to call you His brother or sister?
What might God be forming in you through a hardship you would rather avoid?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The teacher says the lesson exposes a nerve. At 47, raised in the church, he learned to pray, 'Lord, I'm suffering, please stop it immediately.' Asking for relief is still appropriate, and he has prayed it for his parents and himself, but he wonders if he jumps to it too quickly instead of first asking what God may be forming through it. For 17 years he has wrestled with how to pray for his father, a quadriplegic since an accident in 2009 whom God has not healed. About four years ago his youngest son prayed, 'Lord, please let Grandpa walk again,' and he broke down; he realized he had assumed God would either heal immediately or never, with no frame for the purpose of suffering and union with Christ. He has watched his father soften into a man who truly loves the Lord, and his mother make the same journey, through what they have endured. Hebrews 2 won't let him treat suffering as meaningless. Maybe the prayer is: 'Lord, meet me here. Form Christ in me. Teach me to trust You here. And if You do not remove this suffering today, don't let it be wasted.'
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): take one hardship you are praying about and write two prayers, one asking for relief and one asking God to form Christ in you through it. Pray both this week.

## Summary (from the video)

- Observations: 'But we do see Him' answers 2:8. We don't yet see humanity ruling as Psalm 8 describes, but we see Jesus, the true, representative human who fulfills mankind's destiny. His suffering and death were 'by the grace of God', the sovereign, gracious plan of God, not an accident. In verse 10 the subject is God the Father: 'it was fitting' points back to 'by the grace of God'. Yet Hebrews 1 ties creation to the Son, so the author assumes both distinction and unity in God without stopping to explain; the teacher points to the 'two powers in heaven' discussion (Alan Segal; popularized by Michael Heiser).
- 'Perfect' doesn't mean Christ was flawed, but that He completed something: bringing many sons to glory through suffering. The Son is not ashamed to call weak, tempted people brothers. Verse 14 describes the incarnation, and verse 15's slavery, death and deliverance has a new-Exodus flavor, preparing for Moses in chapter 3: Jesus is the greater deliverer. Verse 17's priestly language presents Him as the merciful and faithful high priest who makes propitiation.
- Old Testament background: Psalm 8 is still the backdrop for verse 9, and the logic tracks with Romans 5:17, Adam's trespass and the reign of the One, Jesus Christ. Psalm 22, which Jesus quoted on the cross, moves from suffering to vindication and praise among the brothers (2:12). Isaiah and his children were signs in Israel during fear and political crisis, when people were tempted to fear earthly powers rather than trust Yahweh (2:13). Israel's priesthood, sacrifice and atonement stand behind 2:17. In one word, the passage is about solidarity.
- The lesson: 'Suffering is not a detour from human glory. In union with the Son who suffered with us and for us, suffering becomes part of the path by which God brings many sons to glory.' For pressured, weary believers, suffering did not mean God had abandoned them or that Jesus had failed.

### Track the pronouns
In Hebrews 2:9-11 mark every 'He', 'Him' and 'His' and decide who each refers to: the Father, the Son, or the brothers. Then do the same in 1:1-3 and see how the author speaks of the Father and the Son together.

- Jesus: Made for a little while lower than the angels, crowned because of the suffering of death; the author of salvation and merciful high priest (2:9-17). [Background] The first time Hebrews uses the name Jesus (2:9).
- God the Father: The subject of 2:10: for whom and through whom are all things, bringing many sons to glory. [Background] Chrysostom also reads 2:10 of the Father (see Early witnesses).
- The devil: The one who had the power of death, rendered powerless through Jesus' death (2:14). [Background] See 1 John 3:8.
- Abraham's seed: Those Jesus helps, rather than angels (2:16). [Background] God's people, heirs of the promise to Abraham.
- Isaiah and his children: Signs in Israel during a time of fear and crisis (Isaiah 8:18). [Background] His sons' names were themselves signs (Isaiah 7:3; 8:3).
- Aaron: Behind the priestly language of 2:17. [Background] Israel's first high priest (Exodus 28).

## Places [Background]
- Egypt (named in the video): Slavery and deliverance: the new-Exodus pattern behind 2:15.
- Mount Zion: Where Yahweh of hosts dwells (Isaiah 8:18); Isaiah's children were signs in Jerusalem.

## Key terms
- Perfect (teleioō): To complete or bring to the goal, not to fix a flaw (2:10).
- Incarnation: The Son taking on flesh and blood (2:14).
- Propitiation: The sacrifice that turns away God's wrath and deals with sin (2:17).
- New Exodus: God's greater deliverance, patterned on the rescue from Egypt.
- Two powers in heaven: Ancient Jewish discussion of a second divine figure alongside Yahweh; studied by Alan Segal.
- Solidarity: The teacher's one-word summary: Jesus fully shares our condition.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- The high priest: Israel's high priest represented the people before God and, on the Day of Atonement, brought sacrificial blood into the most holy place (Leviticus 16). Hebrews introduces Jesus as high priest here and develops it from chapter 4 on.
- Fear of death in the ancient world: Death was feared across the ancient world, and philosophers wrote to help people face it. Hebrews names fear of death as a slavery that Jesus breaks by entering death Himself.
- Two powers in heaven: Alan Segal's study traced rabbinic objections to teachers who spoke of a second divine power in heaven. Michael Heiser argued the idea has roots in the Old Testament itself, where Yahweh can be distinguished from Yahweh.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 400): "That by the grace of God He should taste death for every man, not for the faithful only, but even for the whole world: for He indeed died for all;" Homilies on Hebrews 4, on 2:9. NPNF 1.14 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 400): "To make perfect through sufferings. Then sufferings are a perfecting, and a cause of salvation. Do you see that to suffer affliction is not the portion of those who are utterly forsaken;" Homilies on Hebrews 4, on 2:10. NPNF 1.14 (public domain). Earlier in the homily he says of 2:10, 'He speaks here of the Father.'
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 400): "For this cause (he means) He took on Him our flesh, only for Love to man, that He might have mercy upon us." Homilies on Hebrews 5, on 2:17. NPNF 1.14 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Propitiation or expiation? (2:17) Hilaskomai can mean turning away God's wrath (propitiation, as in the LSB) or wiping away sin (expiation). C. H. Dodd argued for expiation; many since have argued that both ideas are present.
- How was Jesus made perfect? (2:10; 5:9) Interpreters agree it isn't moral improvement. Some stress vocational completion (qualified as Savior and priest through suffering); others stress His human obedience reaching its goal in death and exaltation.
- 'For everyone' (2:9) Chrysostom read 'taste death for everyone' as the whole world. Others read it within the letter's focus on the 'many sons' and 'brothers'. The verse figures in wider debates about the scope of the atonement.

## Careful reading notes
Small points worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says both quotations in 2:13 come from Isaiah 8:17. The second, 'Behold, I and the children', is Isaiah 8:18. The first follows the Greek of 8:17; the LSB, translating the Hebrew, reads 'I will hope for Him'.
- The video reads Psalm 8:5 as 'a little lower than the heavenly beings'; the LSB, like Hebrews 2:9, has 'angels'. The Hebrew word ('elohim) allows both.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. What do you usually pray first when you or someone you love is suffering?
2. How does 'we do see Him' (2:9) answer 'we do not yet see' (2:8)?
3. What does it mean that Jesus was 'perfected' without ever being flawed?
4. Where do you need to hear that the Son is not ashamed to call you His brother or sister?
5. What might God be forming in you through a hardship you would rather avoid?

## Application
- (video) The teacher says the lesson exposes a nerve. At 47, raised in the church, he learned to pray, 'Lord, I'm suffering, please stop it immediately.' Asking for relief is still appropriate, and he has prayed it for his parents and himself, but he wonders if he jumps to it too quickly instead of first asking what God may be forming through it. For 17 years he has wrestled with how to pray for his father, a quadriplegic since an accident in 2009 whom God has not healed. About four years ago his youngest son prayed, 'Lord, please let Grandpa walk again,' and he broke down; he realized he had assumed God would either heal immediately or never, with no frame for the purpose of suffering and union with Christ. He has watched his father soften into a man who truly loves the Lord, and his mother make the same journey, through what they have endured. Hebrews 2 won't let him treat suffering as meaningless. Maybe the prayer is: 'Lord, meet me here. Form Christ in me. Teach me to trust You here. And if You do not remove this suffering today, don't let it be wasted.'
- Study note (added): take one hardship you are praying about and write two prayers, one asking for relief and one asking God to form Christ in you through it. Pray both this week.
